reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story: Josephine sat down for soup time at daycare. Her bowl was big. Max had a small cup. The soup was hot. Steam went up, up, up. Josephine wanted to eat now. "Too hot," said Teacher Ann. "We wait." So Josephine waited. She gave her teddy bear a kiss. Then she touched the side of her bowl. Still hot. Max touched his small cup. "Mine is warm now," he said. He ate his soup. It went fast. Josephine touched her big bowl again. Still hot. She waited some more. She watched the steam get small. At last the bowl felt warm. "The big bowl got cold slow," said Josephine. "The small cup got cold fast." She took a big bite. "Yum," she said. "Worth the wait."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Alexis sat at the big table. He had a heavy red truck in his pocket. Mom had helped him wash his hands before dinner. His ears could hear the spoons clink.

At school, Mia had grabbed the truck. Alexis had grabbed it back. Then Mia cried. Then Alexis cried too. The teacher gave the truck a spot on the shelf. She said they could each have a turn. Alexis waited. He counted to ten. Mia pushed the truck down the ramp. Then Alexis had his turn. He pushed it too. The truck rolled far. Mia clapped.

"Dinner is ready," said Dad. Alexis put the truck on the table. "Mia, your turn," he said. He slid the truck to his baby sister. She laughed and held it with both hands. Alexis counted to ten. One, two, three. His sister gave the truck back. "My turn," said Alexis. He made the truck drive over the bread.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Jacob stood in the bathroom. His new toothbrush was lost. "I want my blue toothbrush," he said. Daddy was there, brushing his own teeth.

Jacob looked with his eyes. He saw the sink. He saw the big mirror. No toothbrush. He listened with his ears. He heard water drip, drip, drip. No toothbrush. He touched the furry bath mat with his hands. It was soft. No toothbrush there. He sniffed with his nose. He smelled Daddy's minty toothpaste. "Mmm," said Jacob.

Then Jacob closed his eyes to guess. He reached for his cup. He missed it. The cup fell over. Clang! "Oh," said Jacob. "I missed it because my eyes were shut." He opened his eyes and picked it up. There, behind the cup, was the blue toothbrush! Jacob smiled. He put a little paste on it. He brushed his teeth. His tongue tasted the mint. "Minty," he said. Daddy said, "All clean, little man." Jacob spat, rinsed, and held Daddy's hand all the way to bed.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Ivy went to the library with Dad. She wanted to draw a cat on the new tablet. Dad said, "First you press the little round button." Ivy pressed it. The screen stayed dark. "Oh no," said Ivy. "The cat is asleep!" Dad laughed.

Then Dad showed her the button on top. Ivy slid it to the side. The screen woke up. "The button has to say green," said Ivy. She tapped the green dot. A picture of a paint brush came up. She tapped it. Now she could draw! She drew a cat with big ears and a hat.

At the end, Dad said, "Time to put it away." Ivy pressed the top button again. The screen went dark. She put the tablet in its basket. "In summer I will draw the cat again," she said. Dad said, "It will remember your cat." Ivy whispered, "Good night, cat."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: watching a big game with family and friends
story:
Jaxon put on his red hat. The big game was on TV today! Aunt May came with chips. Grandpa came with a whistle. Even the boy next door came to watch.

Then the TV went dark. "Oh no," said Jaxon. "The game is lost!" Everyone looked for the problem. Grandpa looked behind the couch. Jaxon looked under the rug. He found his toy turtle there, but no game.

Jaxon marched into the kitchen. There was Dad, holding the TV plug. "The fan needed the plug," said Dad. "So the TV went off." One plug, one dark TV. Jaxon got it. "Put it back, Dad!" he yelled. Dad plugged in the TV. The game came back, big and bright.

The crowd on TV got loud. The buzzer went beep, beep, beep. "That means someone scored!" said Jaxon. Grandpa blew his little whistle. Aunt May jumped up. Chips went everywhere. Jaxon hugged his turtle and cheered too. "We win," he said. "All of us!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to spread butter on toast and pour milk into a cup without spilling
story:
Ezra went to the farmers' market with Dad. They bought warm bread and fresh milk. A farmer gave Ezra a cup of juice too.

At home, Dad cut the warm bread into toast. "Can I teach you to butter it?" Dad asked. Ezra took the knife. He pushed hard. The toast tore. "Why did it rip?" Ezra asked. Dad gave him a new piece. The toast was warm and soft. Ezra touched it. The butter went soft too. It sat flat on the bread. He slid the knife gently. The butter spread all over. "Warm toast makes butter soft," Ezra said. He said it again. "Warm toast makes butter soft!"

Then Ezra poured the milk. He held the cup up high. Milk splashed out. He put the cup on the table, low and still. He poured slowly. Not one drop spilled. "Low cup, slow pour," said Ezra. He poured Dad's milk next. Not one drop.

Dad took a big bite of toast. "Mmm," said Dad. "More, please."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Leah went to the library with her mom. She wanted a book about dogs. Leah loved dogs. She loved their soft fur and wet noses.

She looked on a shelf. She found books about bears, cats and ducks. "So many animals," said Leah. The animal books all sat together on one shelf. That was why she could not find dogs at first. Dogs were animals too! Dogs were with the cats!

Next to that shelf was a shelf of toys. Cars, balls and blocks had their own books too. Then Leah found a shelf of food books. Apples, bread and eggs sat together in a big picture book.

Then Leah saw a book with a face on it. The face had a big nose and ugly green bumps. "What is that?" she asked. It was a book about frogs! Leah patted the frog picture. "Hello, frog," she said. "You are an animal too. You sit with the dogs."

Mom smiled. "Which book do you want, Leah?" Leah held the dog book in one hand. She held the frog book in the other hand. "Both," said Leah. "Animals are my favorite."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Sienna sat at the big camp table. She was making a sun out of paper. The sun needed yellow paper, glue, and a paper bag for the scraps.

First she cut a big circle. Then she squeezed the glue bottle. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. So much glue came out! The paper got very wet and shiny.

She spread the glue with her hand. Now her hand was dirty and sticky. "Sticky, sticky, sticky," she sang. Her friend Leo laughed. "Your hand is a glue hand!" he said.

Then Sienna tried to pick up her sun. The wet paper tore. "Oh no!" she said. "My sun ripped!"

She looked at the torn sun. Then she looked at the glue bottle. She thought and thought. "Too much glue makes paper wet," she said. "Wet paper rips!"

Next she made a new sun. This time she made one small dot of glue. Just one dot. The paper stayed dry. The sun did not rip. It was a good sun.

Leo held up his art. His paper had ripped too. There was a hole right in the middle. But Leo grinned and peeked through the hole with one eye. "Look!" he said. "My ripped paper is a mask!"

Sienna peeked through her old torn sun too. "Two masks!" she said. Then she hung her new sun on the wall, right up high.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Jasper wanted to feed the fish in his little tank. He put his hand in the toy box. He pulled out a toy banana. He held it over the water.

"Fish do not eat toy bananas," said Grandma. "Toys are not food."

Jasper looked at the banana. It was hard and shiny. It could not be lunch. He had a problem now. What do fish eat?

He went to the kitchen with Grandma. He saw real food there. Apples, bread, and a small can of fish flakes. "I guess the fish eat this," Jasper said.

He was gentle with the little flakes. He dropped three into the tank. The fish swam fast. It gobbled them up.

"Toys are for playing," said Jasper. "Food is for eating." The fish wiggled its tail at him.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: making an art or craft project
story:
Lea sat at the big art table. She was making a picture of a cat. One cat, two ears, three whiskers on each side. She squeezed the glue bottle to stick on paper eyes. Squeeze, squeeze, squeeze. The glue came out like a white river.

Lea pressed the paper eyes down. They slid off. She pressed again. They slid again. The paper got wet and floppy. Lea felt worried. "My cat is falling apart," she said. Miss Amy came over. She sat close by Lea. "Let's look together," she said.

Lea looked at the glue bottle. It was almost full when she started. Now it was nearly empty. "I used too much glue," Lea said. "Wet glue makes paper slip and slide." Miss Amy smiled. "Yes. A little dot will hold," she said.

Miss Amy helped Lea cut a new cat. Lea made one small dot for each eye. One dot, two dots, three dots for the whiskers. She waited a bit. The glue got sticky, not wet. The eyes stayed on. The cat was done, just as the bell rang for snack. Miss Amy said, "You can cook your lunch story later, and this little cat can come too." Lea hugged the cat to her chest. "He is my baby cat," she said. "He will ride in my bag."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Ellie sat at the big table. Everyone was there. Grandma was there. Grandpa was there too.

The food smelled good. Ellie wanted to eat now. But Mom held her hand and said, "We wait. We say our blessing first."

Ellie folded her hands like Mom. But she did not know the words. She looked down at her plate. Everyone was quiet and waiting.

Grandpa smiled at her. He said the words slowly. "Thank you for our food." Ellie listened. Grandpa said the words again. "Thank you for our food."

Ellie tried too. "Thank you for... food," she said. Her words were a little different. But that was okay. Grandpa clapped. "Good try, Ellie!"

Then everyone said it together. "Thank you for our food." Ellie said it with them. She said every word. "The food comes after the words," Ellie said. "First we say it. Then we eat."

Mom kissed her head. "That's right, Ellie." The bowls went around the table. Grandpa put warm rice in Ellie's bowl.

After dinner, Ellie helped Mom bathe the baby. She sang the blessing to him. "Thank you for our food." The baby kicked his feet in the water.

"Say it again," said Grandpa from the door.

Ellie said it again.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: going to the dentist for the first time
story:
Sofia climbed into the car. She held her favorite toy bunny. "Today I see the dentist!" she said. "Hurry, Daddy, hurry!"

Daddy drove fast but safe. Sofia looked out the window. She saw the dentist building. It had a big tooth on the sign!

The dentist had a little mirror on a stick. "Open wide," she said. Sofia opened her mouth very wide. The mirror bounced light inside. Now the dentist could see all the way back. "I can count your teeth!" she said. "One, two, three, all the way to twenty!"

"Twenty!" said Sofia. "I have twenty teeth because I opened wide!"

Then the dentist gave her a sticker. But that was not all. In the box was a tiny tooth toy for bunny! Sofia laughed and held it up. "Bunny opened wide too," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
story:
Rehmat sat on the playroom floor. She wanted her teddy. She could not find him. "Do not worry," said Mama. "Let us look."

Rehmat put two cars on the ramp. The big car went down fast. The small car went down slow. "Big car is fast!" she said. Then she saw it. The big car had stopped by a big box. The big box was too heavy to lift. Rehmat felt grumpy. Her teddy was inside, she was sure.

Mama helped her tip the box over. Out came teddy, warm from sitting near the sunny window. Rehmat touched him. "Teddy is hot," she said. Mama brought a cool cloth. Soon teddy felt cold and nice. On teddy's paw was a letter, the letter R, just like her name. Rehmat pointed at it and laughed. "R is for Rehmat!" She hugged teddy tight and sat close to Mama.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Parker was at Grandma's house. He wanted to make pancakes for his family. Grandma said, "Let's cook them together."

Parker mixed the flour and milk. Then he poured batter into the hot pan. The pancake came out pale and soft. Grandma said, "It is not done yet. Watch the bubbles." Parker waited. Little bubbles popped up all over the top. "Now flip it," said Grandma. Parker flipped it with the spatula. The other side turned golden brown. "The bubbles mean it is ready to flip," said Parker. Grandma smiled.

Then Parker saw a bird at the window. It was building a nest in the big blue pot by the door. "The bird needs some string," said Parker. He put soft string on the step. The bird took it for her nest.

Dad came in from the porch. He had let his bike ride down the hill and back. "Something smells good," said Dad. Parker set the table with blue plates. Everyone ate the pancakes. Dad took a big bite and said, "These are the best ones yet."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Weston wanted to play house in the backyard. He set his teddy bear on a square blanket. "You be my baby," he said. Weston stirred dirt and water in a pot. That was pretend soup for lunch.

Then teddy fell off the blanket. He landed in the wet grass. Weston ran to him. "Are you okay?" he asked. He hugged teddy close. "Sorry I put you near the edge," he said. Weston found out why teddy fell. The blanket was on a hill. The hill made teddy slide down.

So Weston moved the blanket to the flat square of patio. He set teddy in the middle. "Now you will stay," he said. Mom sat on the step and watched. Weston fed teddy his pretend soup, one spoonful at a time. "Time for bed, baby," Weston whispered.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Audrey sat on the little red mat. She wanted to find a book about bears. But she could not read the words yet. Her arm reached up to a shelf, and she pulled down a big book. It was stuck between two others, so she tugged it free.

On the cover was a letter she knew. It was B. "B says buh," she said softly. She looked at the word under it. The first letter was B. "Buh, buh, bear!" she said. She had found the bear book.

Then she did it again. A book with D on the front. "D says duh," she said. "Duh, duh, dog!" That one was about dogs. Audrey hugged the book. "The first letter tells me," she whispered. She carried both books to the cozy corner to read.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Sadie ran to the playground with her grandma. The sun was hot on the slide. Sadie put her hand near it. The slide felt hot, too. "Ouch," said Sadie. She pulled her hand back fast.

Grandma sat on a short bench under a tree. Sadie wanted to slide. She waited. She touched the slide again. Still hot. She waited some more. A cloud came and covered the sun. Sadie touched the slide one more time. Now it felt cool. "The sun made it hot," said Sadie. "The cloud made it cool." She climbed up and slid down. Whee!

Then Sadie saw something shiny in the sand. It was a piece of glass. She almost picked it up. But glass can cut fingers. Sadie did not touch it. She ran to grandma and held her hand. They walked back together, slow and easy.

A little dog ran by. It turned around and licked Sadie's nose. Sadie laughed and laughed. "Again," she said. "Do it again."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Aubrey sat in the school computer lab. In front of her was a black tablet. It did not look at her. It was dark and still.

"I want to draw a cat," said Aubrey.

The teacher said, "Try the little round button."

Aubrey found the button on the side. She pushed it. She waited. She counted, "One, two, three." The screen woke up. It was bright. The tablet was on because she pushed the button! "I did it," said Aubrey.

Next she looked for the drawing app. She saw a little orange square. She tapped it with one finger. The page opened. It was white and empty. Aubrey picked a green color. Then she picked yellow. The green and yellow mixed into something new on the screen. It looked like grass in the sun. She drew a big cat on the grass.

A boy next to her had a dark screen. He looked sad. Aubrey showed him her button. He pushed it and counted, "One, two, three." His screen woke up too.

Then it was time to go. The teacher said, "Put the tablets away."

Aubrey pressed the top button. The screen went dark. She slid the tablet into the soft blue basket, just like that. "Bye bye, cat," she said.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Alexander wanted to draw with his new pencil. Mom was cooking soup in the kitchen. The pot went "pssss" on the hot stove. Alexander stood next to Mom. He held her apron with one hand.

"Can I see the soup?" he asked. "You can look from here," said Mom. "The pot is hot. Hot things can hurt you." Alexander looked at the steam. The steam went up like a little cloud. He put his hand near, but not close. He felt warm air. He pulled his hand back. "It is hot because the stove makes it hot," said Alexander. Mom smiled. "Yes, that is right."

Then Alexander sat at the table. He drew the pot and the steam with his pencil. He drew Mom too. Mom put a cold cup of water beside him. He touched the cup. It felt cold. "Cold is safe for my hands," he said. Mom clapped. "You learned something new today!" The sun came in the window. It was a sunny day, and the soup smelled good. "Lunch is ready," said Mom.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
story:
Josephine ran straight to the story corner at the library. Today was song day! But the singing lady was not there yet. Josephine wanted to sing "One, two, buckle my shoe." She could not remember what came next.

She looked on the shelf. She pulled out one red book. Then two books. Then three, four, five. Soon her pile was very big. The singing lady came in and laughed. "What a big pile!" she said. "Let's count it together."

They pointed and sang. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The numbers came out in the same order every time! Josephine said, "The words go in a line, like the books!"

She stacked the books in a straight, tall tower. Then she found a book about doctors and medicine to take home. "Ten books is too many," said the singing lady. Josephine giggled and put eight back. "Two to keep," she said. "One, two!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: learning to play a musical instrument
story:
Julia went to the band room at school. She saw a big drum, a small drum, and a shiny flute. Julia wanted to play the big drum. Its name was Boomer. The teacher let her try.

Julia hit Boomer very, very hard. The sound was so loud. She jumped back and put her hands over her ears. The loud boom made her friend Sam cry. Sam was upset. Julia was upset too. She did not want to hurt his ears.

Julia looked at her drumstick. She tried again. She tapped Boomer soft and slow. Boooom. A gentle sound came out. Then she tapped a little harder. The boom got a little bigger. Julia smiled. "Soft tap, small boom," she said. "Hard hit, big boom!"

Sam came close. Julia handed him a drumstick. "Tap soft," she said. Sam tapped soft. The drum said boooom, nice and low. Sam laughed and laughed. Julia gave him a hug.

Then they tapped together, soft, soft, soft. Boomer sang like thunder far away.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to recognise the letters of the alphabet and the sound each letter makes
story:
Evan ran to Grandma's fridge. Magnets lived there, all different letters. Evan wanted to find the letter E. It was his letter, the first letter of his name.

He searched and searched. So many letters! He found M and A. He found a B that looked a bit shy, hiding behind a pot. Then he saw it. E! He jumped up and down. "Grandma, I found E!" He held it high like a trophy.

"E says eh," said Evan, and he said it loud. "Eh, eh, eh, like Evan!" Grandma laughed and clapped. A feather from her hat floated down. Evan tried to catch it. It made him laugh too. Then he climbed onto a chair and put the E right at the top of the fridge. "E for Evan stays up high," he said. "The E found me because it has three little lines, and I know it now!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
story:
The big blue bookmobile came to Matthew's street. Matthew held his mama's hand. He had a new card in his fist. It was his very first library card.

"I want a book about trucks," said Matthew. The librarian found a red truck book. Matthew hugged it tight. "This book is mine now," he said. "I keep it forever."

"You can take it home," said the librarian. "But you must bring it back. Then other kids can read it too."

Matthew held the truck book close. He did not want to let it go. At bedtime he read it three times. In the morning, he read it again.

The next week, the bookmobile came back. Beep, beep! Matthew ran to the door. He gave the truck book to the librarian.

A girl was there. She took the truck book. She sat down to read it. "She likes my truck book," said Matthew. He gave a big smile.

Mama helped him pick a new book. It was about a duck. A loose duck feather fell out of the pages. "A feather!" said Matthew.

The bookmobile drove away. Matthew waved. "Come back soon!" he called. He began to sing a little duck song. His mama sang too, all the way home.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: starting the first day of school
story:
Henry ran into his classroom. His backpack was heavy. It had crayons and a toy car inside.

Henry looked at the wall. Many little boxes sat there. Each box had a name on it. Henry put his backpack in a box. Then a girl came. "That is my box," she said. "It says Mia."

Henry looked. Yes. The name said Mia. "Where is my box?" he asked. Mia pointed. "Find your name."

Henry walked slow. He touched each name with his finger. Sam. Nina. Ben. Then he saw it. Henry. His name was on a blue box.

"My name is on my box," Henry said. "That is how I know it is mine." He put his heavy backpack inside. The box was just right.

Later the teacher said, "Time for pretend play." Henry grabbed a kit. It had a bandage in it. "I will be the doctor," he said. "My teddy has a sick paw."

Mia held out the teddy. "Can you fix him?" she asked.

"Yes," said Henry. "I will touch his paw. Then he gets a bandage." He stuck it on. The teddy looked very brave.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
story:
Myles sat at the little table in art class. Sun came in the window. It was a sunny day. Myles wanted to make a paper boat. He wanted it to roll to his friend Sam.

Myles cut a square for the boat. Then he cut two more squares for wheels. He taped them on. He pushed the boat. The boat did not roll. It stopped. It tipped over on its side.

Myles looked across the room. Mia had a toy car. Her car rolled far. Myles looked at the wheels. Her wheels were round like a ball. "Your wheels are circles," Myles said. Mia smiled. "Circles roll," she said.

Myles cut two circles. He taped them on his boat. He pushed the boat again. The boat rolled across the table. It rolled right to Sam. Sam laughed and clapped.

"My boat rolls now," said Myles. "The squares made it stop. The circles make it go." He hopped down from his chair. He rolled the boat back home. The round wheels went round and round.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
story:
Grace sat in the big chair at the dentist. The dentist had a fuzzy puppet with big white teeth. Grace held it and laughed.

Then the dentist said, "You get a cookie after your checkup." Grace wanted that cookie very much. But the dentist said, "First, wash your hands."

Grace looked at her hands. They looked clean. "Do germs hide on them?" she asked.

"Let's find out," said the dentist. He took her to the sink. Grace put soap on her hands. The dentist said, "Now we count to twenty." Grace rubbed and counted. One, two, three. The bubbles grew soft and white. At twenty, she rinsed. The bubbles and germs went down the drain.

"I get it," said Grace. "The soap needs time to catch the germs." She dried her hands and ate her cookie. It tasted sweet.

After the cookie, Grace drank her cup of ice water. "Do I wash again after the toilet too?" she asked.

"Yes," said the dentist. "Twenty seconds, every time." Grace smiled at the fuzzy puppet. "Ready, germs? Nowhere to hide!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Ibrahim went to Zayd's house. Zayd had a tablet. Ibrahim wanted to draw on it. But the screen was dark and still. He tapped it. Nothing happened. He tapped again. Still nothing.

"Press the round button," said Zayd. "Hold it down." Ibrahim pressed the little round button. He held his finger there. One, two, three. The screen lit up, bright and warm like sunshine. "It woke up!" said Ibrahim. "My finger made it wake up."

Zayd showed him a green square with a crayon on it. "Tap this," he said. "It is the drawing app." Ibrahim tapped it. Now he could draw. He drew a big red circle. He drew a silly cat with three eyes. "Your cat looks surprised," laughed Zayd. Ibrahim drew a blue square shape next. Then a yellow one. "I learn fast," he said proudly.

When he finished, the tablet began to blink. "Oh no, it is tired," said Ibrahim. "Batteries get low," said Zayd. "We must put it away." Ibrahim pressed the round button again. The screen went dark. He set the tablet on the shelf, soft and safe. "Sorry, tablet," he whispered. "Sleep well, tired friend."

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
story:
Jayden wanted to give his mom a present. He found a small ice cube in his cup. "This can be my present," he said. He put it in his hand.

The ice felt very cold. Jayden shivered a little. Then he saw steam rising from the pot on the stove. The pot was hot. He did not touch the pot. Mama had told him, hot things can hurt you.

Jayden wanted to show Mama his ice present. He walked to the door. Then he remembered, stay close to Mama. So he stayed in the kitchen. He sat down on his little stool.

The ice began to melt in his warm hand. Drip, drip, drip. Soon there was only water. "Oh no," said Jayden. "My ice is gone."

Mama looked at his wet hand. "The ice melted because your hand is warm," she said. "Would you like a new present to give me?" Jayden nodded. They picked a red crayon together. Jayden drew a big red heart. He gave the paper to Mama. "A present for you," he said. Mama smiled and put it on the door.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
story:
Joshua went to Mia's house. Mia had a big toy kitchen. Joshua wanted to make soup too.

Mia said, "First we need a pot." She put the pot on the little stove. Joshua put in a red ball. That was the tomato.

Joshua stirred and stirred. He used a big wooden spoon. Round and round went the spoon.

"Where is the door to the oven?" Joshua asked. Mia pointed. Joshua peeked in. Oh! The oven was cold. Was that okay? Mia said the pretend oven could not get hot. That is why it was safe.

Then Baby Bear got sick. Joshua held Baby Bear. "Baby needs a nap," he said. He patted Baby Bear's back, soft and slow. Baby Bear's eyes closed.

"Why did Baby Bear go to sleep?" Joshua wondered. He patted again. Slow patting made Baby Bear sleepy. Fast patting woke Baby Bear up! Joshua laughed.

He patted slow, slow, slow. Baby Bear slept and slept. Baby looked so tired after the long day.

Joshua gave Baby Bear a blanket. He made pretend soup for Mia too. Round and round, the spoon went swish.

Then Daddy Bear came home. Mia made a big voice, "I'm home!" Joshua ran to the door. He opened it wide.

Daddy Bear said, "Something smells good!"

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to turn on a tablet, open a drawing app and put it away when done
story:
Charlotte was at Mia's house. Mia had a tablet on the rug. Charlotte wanted to draw a big hill on it. But the screen was dark and blank.

Mia said, "Press the little button on top." Charlotte pressed it. The screen lit up. "The button makes it turn on," said Charlotte.

She pressed the round blue spot. The drawing app opened. Charlotte drew a green hill and a yellow sun. She took her time. She drew a small cat on the hill too.

Then the drawing was done. "Now we put it away," said Mia. Charlotte pressed the button again. The screen went dark. She heard the soft click.

"Can I do it one more time?" asked Charlotte. "Yes," said Mia. "The button works every time." Charlotte pressed it, and the sun came back.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
story:
Sarah ran into the library. She wanted a puppy book! "Where are the puppy books?" she asked Mom.

Mom pointed to a big shelf. Sarah saw a picture of a cat on a sign. She bent down to look. Cat books, bunny books, bird books! All the animals sat on one shelf.

But one book was in the wrong spot. It was a book about cake. Cake is food, not an animal! Sarah held it. The cover felt rough. She carried it to the food shelf. Apples, bread, milk, all together.

"The cake book goes here," said Sarah. "Animals go with animals. Food goes with food."

A librarian smiled. "Thank you, Sarah!"

Sarah ran back to the animal shelf. She found the puppy book! She hugged it tight.

"Puppy books live with the animals," she said. "That is why I found him!"

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
story:
Max sat at the kitchen table. He wanted to write his name. His brother had a new pencil for him.

Max grabbed the pencil in his whole fist. He tried to write an M. The pencil wobbled. The M looked like a squiggle. Max frowned at it.

He watched his brother write. His brother held the pencil near the tip. He used just two fingers and his thumb. Max looked at his own hand. He held his pencil way up high, far from the point. He slid his fingers down, close to the tip. He pinched it with two fingers and his thumb.

Max wrote an M. It did not wobble. "It holds still now," Max said. "My fingers are close to the point." He wrote an A, then an X. He wrote M-A-X three more times.

The ink had to dry, so Max waited. Then he held the paper up. "Look, brother! It says Max!"

story:
Nicholas wanted to play house at Grandma's house. He looked for a baby doll. He found a box under Grandma's bed. He counted the dolls inside. "One, two, three," he said. But all the dolls looked grumpy. Their faces were flat and sad.

"Why are the dolls sad?" he asked. Grandma said, "Maybe they need a mama." Nicholas tried holding a doll like a baby. He wrapped it in a small towel. He rocked it in his arms. Then the doll's head fell back. It looked right at him with a smile. The towel made the head stay up!

Nicholas picked up the second doll. He wrapped it too. He rocked it and sang a little song. Grandma clapped her hands. "The towel makes the head stay up," said Nicholas. "Now all my babies can smile." He gave the third doll a big hug.

story:
Willow ran to the play corner at school. She wanted to play house. Her friend Milo was there too. "You be the dad," said Willow. "I will be the mom."

Willow picked up the baby doll. The doll's eyes were open. "The baby is awake," said Willow. "She needs a nap."

She wrapped the doll in a small blanket. She rocked it in her arms. She sang a soft song. But the doll's eyes would not close. Willow looked at the doll. The eyes stayed open because the doll was lying flat on her knee!

Willow sat the doll up. Then she tipped her back slowly. Click! The eyes shut. "The baby is asleep," said Willow.

Milo tiptoed over. "Shh," he said. "Let's make soup now." Willow smiled and put the doll in the little bed.

activity: to share a toy with a classmate and wait for a turn without grabbing
story:
Gianna was at Milo's birthday party. A big dig truck sat on the toy table. It had a long arm and a scoop. Gianna wanted it. She grabbed for it. But Ben had it first. He held on tight. The truck stopped moving.

"You both pulled," said Milo's mom. "The truck has to wait for calm hands." Gianna let go. She sat on her hands. "Can we take turns?" she asked. "Yes," said Ben. "You can dig the sand first."

Gianna dug a hole with the scoop. She piled the sand thin and tall. Then she gave the truck to Ben. He made a big hill. Then it was her turn again. "Why does the truck work now?" she asked. "Because we take turns!" she said. Turn, turn, turn. They played until the cake came out.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
story:
Olivia went to the garden center with Dad. She held a little tray of seeds. The sun was warm on her nose. There were tomatoes, carrots, and beans. Olivia wanted to grow beans best.

She filled a pot with soft brown soil. Her hands smelled like dirt and rain. She pushed three bean seeds into the pot. Then she set the pot in the shade under a table. Dad said, "Put it in the sun, too." So Olivia put the pot in a sunny spot.

A loud truck came by the gate. It dropped off many bags of soil. The truck honked and rolled away. Olivia did not jump this time. Dad was holding her hand.

Every day Olivia gave the pot a little water. On day five, a green sprout popped up. It bent toward the sunny window. "Look, Dad! It is leaning to the light!" Olivia turned the pot around. The next day the sprout bent back to the sun. "The sun pulls it," she said.

But then the hot weather came. One leaf turned brown and dry. "Dad, the leaf burns in the hot sun!" Dad nodded. "So we move it to the shade at noon." They moved the pot together. The leaf rested in the cool shade. Olivia patted the soil gently. "Grow, little bean," she said. "I will keep you safe." The sprout stood tall and green in the evening light.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: to say a family blessing or greeting before a shared meal
story:
Ivy came to the cemetery with Mama and Nana. They brought a picnic basket. They sat on a dry, soft blanket near Grandpa Ben's stone. The stone felt warm in the sun.

Nana opened the basket. She took out bread, cheese, and little cakes. "We eat first," said Ivy, reaching for a cake. Mama held her hand gently. "Wait," said Mama. "At Grandpa Ben's stone, we say our family blessing first. We say thank you before we eat."

Nana held out her hands. Ivy put her small hands in theirs. One hand was warm. One hand was soft. "Now we all say it together," said Nana. Nana said the words. Mama said the words. Ivy did not know the words yet. She listened. "Thank you for the sun. Thank you for the food. Thank you for family."

Then Nana said, "Now we eat." Ivy picked up a cake. It was sweet and good. "I want to choose a cake for Grandpa Ben," said Ivy. Nana helped her set one little cake on the flat stone. Ivy put her hand on the warm rock. "We hold hands, then we talk, then we eat," said Ivy. Nana gave her a big smile. "Yes," said Nana. "That is how our blessing goes." Ivy licked the crumbs from her fingers. "Again next time," she said.

story:
Maverick went to Grandma's house. He heard a little sound. "Waah, waah." It came from the toy box. Grandma held his hand. "It is just your baby doll," she said. "The doll is not really sad. But you can pretend."

Maverick picked up the doll. He held it like Grandma showed him. He gave the doll a bottle. It was empty, but he tipped it anyway. He made a little sip sound. The crying stopped. Maverick looked up big-eyed. "The doll stopped crying because I fed her," he said.

Then he gave the doll a toy pig to hug. The doll patted the pig. "Say thank you," said Maverick. He made the doll's voice soft and polite. "Thank you."

Grandma smiled. She sat in the old swing on the porch. Maverick sat close with his baby. The swing went back and forth. The doll went to sleep. So did the little pig.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
story:
Emma stood at the little table by the tent. Daddy was there too. He had a sharp knife, and he cut the bananas. Emma kept her hands far away from the sharp part.

Now it was Emma's turn to cook. She poured pancake mix into the pan. The pan sat on the camp stove. It was getting hot. Emma waited. A frog hopped by her shoe. She watched the pan, not the frog.

Then Emma saw little holes in the pancake. Bubbles! Big bubbles came up. Daddy said, "Now flip it, Emma." She turned the pancake over with the spatula. It was not runny anymore. It puffed up big and round. "The bubbles made it ready," said Emma. Daddy smiled. They put the pancake on a plate. Emma took a tiny taste. "Yum!" she said. "More for Mommy too!" The frog hopped away into the grass.

reading_level: Use very short, simple sentences (about 5-8 words each) and concrete, everyday words a young child already knows. One simple idea per sentence.
activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
story:
Anna lost her toy robot. She felt sad. "Where did it go?" she asked.

Anna used her eyes to look. She saw the bed. She saw the chair. No robot there. Then Anna used her ears. She heard a little beep, beep. "Is that my robot?" she said. "Yes, it is!" The robot beeped because she had pushed its button before she put it down.

Anna followed the sound. The beeps came from the basket of socks. She used her hands to touch the soft socks. Something hard was under them. She pulled it out. It was her robot!

Anna hugged it. "My nose did not find you," she said. "My ears did!" Then Mommy called, "Snack time!" Anna smelled apples. She used her tongue to taste a sweet bite. She touched the robot's button. Beep, beep!
